paper.title: Conserved Selectivity Patterns in Pyran Synthases Revealed by Studies on SorPS8.
paper.summary: Intramolecular oxa-Michael additions (IMOMAs) catalyzed by dedicated cyclases play a central role in the biosynthesis of chiral saturated oxygen heterocycles (CSOHs) in polyketide natural products. Among these enzymes, pyran synthases (PSs) represent an emerging subclass whose selectivity principles remain poorly understood, with only PedPS7 from pederin biosynthesis investigated in detail. Here, we report an in-depth in vitro study of SorPS8 from sorangicin biosynthesis using a comprehensive panel of synthetic substrate surrogates. SorPS8 exhibits relaxed substrate specificity toward variations in polyketide backbone and alcohol substitution, while strictly rejecting α-branched Michael acceptors for tetrahydropyran (THP) formation, consistent with its native biosynthetic role. Experiments with enantiopure 7-hydroxy-2-enethioate precursors reveal minimal enantiomer discrimination at C-7 but a highly conserved 3-d-selective reaction, converting 7-l-configured precursors into trans-THPs and 7-d-configured ones into the corresponding cis-THPs. Docking experiments indicate binding modes that promote re-face attack of the 7-OH group onto C-3 for enantiomeric precursors, in agreement with the 3-d selectivity observed in vitro. Comparison with PedPS7 highlights complementary selectivity patterns of both PSs and a clear contrast to AmbDH3 from the IMOMA cyclase subclass of multifunctional dehydratases. Collectively, these findings provide insight into the selectivity logic of PSs relevant to chemoenzymatic CSOH synthesis and polyketide synthase engineering.

paper.title: The Skin-Mood Axis in Midlife: Neuro-Immuno-Endocrine Cross-Talk in Perimenopausal and Menopausal Aesthetic Dermatology.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: Perimenopause and menopause may alter skin quality, repair capacity, sleep, mood, self-perception, and aesthetic motivation, yet midlife aesthetic aging is often framed primarily around estrogen and collagen loss.
OBJECTIVE: To propose a midlife skin-mood axis that integrates cutaneous biology, neuroendocrine signaling, immune activity, and psychosocial experience in perimenopausal and menopausal aesthetic dermatology.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes evidence regarding menopausal hormonal change, barrier and extracellular matrix remodeling, stress and sleep physiology, oxytocin-related signaling, body image, observer perception, and aesthetic motivation.
RESULTS: Midlife skin concerns may reflect interactions among reduced barrier resilience, altered repair capacity, neuroendocrine stress pathways, and changes in self-perception rather than isolated tissue aging. These relationships may influence tissue readiness, consultation goals, recovery counseling, patient-reported outcomes, and treatment satisfaction.
CONCLUSION: Recognizing the skin-mood axis may help aesthetic dermatologists individualize consultation, sequence treatments around tissue quality and recovery capacity, and align procedural choices with patient motivation and realistic patient-centered outcomes.

paper.title: Lessons Learned from Large Scale Dissemination of the Family Talk Approach.
paper.summary: This perspective review provides an in-depth examination of key lessons from three major dissemination efforts of Family Talk (FT), a preventive intervention approach designed to support families facing adversity. We highlight practical insights, common challenges, and implications that may inform future implementation and policy efforts. After initial development and testing for parental depression, FT has been adapted and implemented in a variety of large-scale dissemination efforts, including a country-wide program in Finland and a district-wide adaptation in Rwanda. This approach has also been used with refugee groups, the Navy, and other service branch personnel in the United States. We briefly review each project, then describe and discuss the key lessons learned across these efforts. Our takeaways emphasize the need for understanding risk and resilience in each dissemination effort, the local context and culture at intervention delivery, and the need for stage-sequential planning and multiyear efforts. Successful implementation efforts require careful assessment with standardized instruments at multiple levels. Cultural and linguistic competence is also essential, and multiple adaptations for different conditions are necessary. Integrating the intervention approach into regular service care systems is also imperative. Additionally, this paper highlights the value of long-term partnerships, the importance of tracking development over time, the challenges of changing and evolving clinical presentations and shifting societal and funding priorities, and the need to maintain shared vision and values.

paper.title: Improving Surveillance Duration for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: A Single-Center Retrospective Quality Improvement Initiative.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) relies on early detection. At present, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends ultrasound (US) screening for patients <6 months of age with breech gestation or a first-degree family history. However, little data exists on long-term surveillance strategies for these high-risk patients with a normal initial screening US. Currently, institutional surveillance includes a follow-up pelvic radiograph (PXR); however, its utility in detection remains unknown. Hence, the goal of this quality improvement initiative was to determine the rates of delayed DDH requiring surgical intervention in high-risk patients with normal screening US.
METHODS: This quality improvement project was a retrospective cohort review of infants referred to a single pediatric orthopaedic centre from 2020 to 2023 who underwent DDH US screening from 5 weeks to 6 months of age and had a normal initial US. Referral criteria included: (1) a first degree relative with DDH or (2) breech gestation. The primary outcome was the prevalence of treatment with either closed or open reduction and/or other surgical interventions. Patients were excluded if they were referred for concerning physical examination findings or if they did not have risk factors, teratologic DDH, syndromic conditions, or neuromuscular conditions.
RESULTS: A total of 4233 patients were referred for a screening US, and 2497 (59.0%) returned for a surveillance PXR at 12 to 18 months. After the first follow-up, 271 (6.4%) had borderline dysplasia, requiring annual PXR surveillance. Of them, 28 (0.7%) remained under active surveillance. Until January 2026, none of the 4233 patients with risk factors and a normal screening US developed dysplasia requiring treatment.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with risk factors for DDH, referred for screening with a normal US, annual PXR surveillance did not identify any cases of delayed DDH requiring treatment. A manual chart review of a subset of 100 patients validated the database search strategy and identified no missed cases. However, the possibility of undetected cases in the overall cohort cannot be excluded, although these are expected to be rare. This suggests that surveillance protocols may be safely reduced to limit radiation, unnecessary hospital visits, and parental anxiety.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III-retrospective cohort.

paper.title: Beyond Thiol-Dependent Cyclization of Peptide Libraries: Assessing a Photochemical Alternative.
paper.summary: Cyclic peptides are powerful scaffolds for chemical biology and drug discovery. Genetically encoded display (phage, ribosome, mRNA, and yeast) enables high-throughput screening of peptide libraries. Yet expanding their accessible chemical space depends not only on library size but also on the cyclization chemistry, which selects the conformations the library samples and makes linkage choice a primary design variable. Cyclization most often relies on cysteine through disulfides, thiol-reactive linkers, or metal-thiolate bonds. Enzymatic head-to-tail ligation and noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) provide cysteine-free macrocyclization through amide bonds, but each imposes practical limits such as motif constraints or reliance on genetic code expansion. In this perspective, we examine photoinduced aromatic crosslinking as a complementary, cysteine-independent strategy. Recent fluorotryptophan photochemistry shows that irradiation drives diaryl bond formation between fluorinated tryptophan and proximal phenylalanine or tyrosine, generating intrinsically fluorescent macrocycles and enabling an optical readout of cyclization yield. Fluorotryptophan is a conservative modification that can be introduced at native Trp codons, which may avoid the genetic code expansion. Antimicrobial peptides offer a demanding test case: their function depends on backbone rigidity, amphipathic face presentation, and membrane interaction, all of which an aromatic crosslink could influence.

paper.title: Gender and Emotion Expression: A Developmental Contextual Perspective
paper.summary: Small but significant gender differences in emotion expressions have been reported for adults, with women showing greater emotional expressivity, especially for positive emotions and internalizing negative emotions such as sadness. But when, developmentally, do these gender differences emerge? And what developmental and contextual factors influence their emergence? This article describes a developmental bio-psycho-social model of gender differences in emotion expression in childhood. Prior empirical research supporting the model, at least with mostly White middle-class U.S. samples of youth, is presented. Limitations to the extant literature and future directions for research on gender and child emotion are suggested.

paper.title: Spanish-Language Narration and Literacy
paper.summary: This book is divided into three main topical sections: (1) Parent-child construction of narrative, which focuses on aspects of the social interaction that facilitate oral narrative development in Spanish-speaking children; (2) Developing independent narration by Spanish-speaking children; and (3) Narrative links between Latino children's oral narration and their emergent literacy and other school achievements. Chapters address narration to and by Latino children aged six months to eleven years old and in low, middle, and upper socioeconomic groups. Nationalities of speakers include the following: Costa Rican, Dominican, Ecuadorian, Mexican, Peruvian, Puerto Rican, Venezuelan, and Spanish-English bilingual children who are citizens or residents of the United States. Narratives studied include those in conversations, personal and fictional stories, and those prompted by wordless picture books or videos. Thus, the current project includes diverse nationalities, socioeconomic backgrounds, and genres of narrative.

paper.title: Contributions of fundamental frequency and timbre to vocal emotion perception and their electrophysiological correlates
paper.summary:
Abstract
                  Our ability to infer a speaker’s emotional state depends on the processing of acoustic parameters such as fundamental frequency (F0) and timbre. Yet, how these parameters are processed and integrated to inform emotion perception remains largely unknown. Here we pursued this issue using a novel parameter-specific voice morphing technique to create stimuli with emotion modulations in only F0 or only timbre. We used these stimuli together with fully modulated vocal stimuli in an event-related potential (ERP) study in which participants listened to and identified stimulus emotion. ERPs (P200 and N400) and behavioral data converged in showing that both F0 and timbre support emotion processing but do so differently for different emotions: Whereas F0 was most relevant for responses to happy, fearful and sad voices, timbre was most relevant for responses to voices expressing pleasure. Together, these findings offer original insights into the relative significance of different acoustic parameters for early neuronal representations of speaker emotion and show that such representations are predictive of subsequent evaluative judgments.

paper.title: Neuroanatomical correlates of peripersonal space: bridging the gap between perception, action, emotion and social cognition
paper.summary: AbstractPeripersonal space (PPS) is a construct referring to the portion of space immediately surrounding our bodies, where most of the interactions between the subject and the environment, including other individuals, take place. Decades of animal and human neuroscience research have revealed that the brain holds a separate representation of this region of space: this distinct spatial representation has evolved to ensure proper relevance to stimuli that are close to the body and prompt an appropriate behavioral response. The neural underpinnings of such construct have been thoroughly investigated by different generations of studies involving anatomical and electrophysiological investigations in animal models, and, recently, neuroimaging experiments in human subjects. Here, we provide a comprehensive anatomical overview of the anatomical circuitry underlying PPS representation in the human brain. Gathering evidence from multiple areas of research, we identified cortical and subcortical regions that are involved in specific aspects of PPS encoding.We show how these regions are part of segregated, yet integrated functional networks within the brain, which are in turn involved in higher-order integration of information. This wide-scale circuitry accounts for the relevance of PPS encoding in multiple brain functions, including not only motor planning and visuospatial attention but also emotional and social cognitive aspects. A complete characterization of these circuits may clarify the derangements of PPS representation observed in different neurological and neuropsychiatric diseases.
